standard_text: Physical properties of metals and non-metals: lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility, sonority and conductivity; reactions with oxygen (basic and acidic oxides) and with water; rusting and its prevention; uses of metals and non-metals (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 4).

key_big: Metals are shiny, malleable, ductile and conduct.

body_html:
How to think about it

Metals such as iron, copper and aluminium are usually lustrous, hard, malleable (beaten into sheets), ductile (drawn into wires), sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals such as sulphur, carbon and oxygen are usually dull and brittle, and do not conduct (graphite is an exception).

Metals burn to form basic oxides (magnesium oxide turns red litmus blue); non-metals form acidic oxides (sulphur dioxide turns blue litmus red). Iron rusts in moist air; painting, oiling and galvanising prevent rusting.

Example

Copper is drawn into wires. Which property?

drawn into thin wires

Answer: ductility

Example

Burning sulphur: nature of the oxide?

non-metal oxide

Answer: acidic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all non-metals are gases.
  • Calling metal oxides acidic.
  • Thinking iron rusts in dry air.

faq.q: What is the difference between malleability and ductility?
faq.a: Malleability is being beaten into thin sheets; ductility is being drawn into thin wires.
By keeping air and moisture away: painting, oiling, greasing or coating with zinc (galvanising).
